content: There are two critical gaps in most healthcare settings that continue to hinder the development of youth-friendly HIV services and systems. Addressing these gaps is essential to establish effective transitioning protocols as individuals move from pediatric to adolescent and eventually to adult HIV services. This will also enable consistent tracking of adherence, retention, and treatment outcomes in this key population group, which is currently being done inconsistently, if at all. The updated consolidated guidelines must provide clear instructions on the data recording systems required to address these challenges. This includes both paper-based registers and electronic systems. Additionally, there is a need for well-defined guidelines, protocols, and recommendations regarding counseling content to standardize approaches for supporting transition, adherence, and retention among adolescents. Further guidance is required on service integration, particularly the integration of sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services, along with recommendations on how facilities can effectively address challenges related to disclosure of HIV status. These findings also raise several key research questions that should shape the future research agenda for adolescent HIV treatment and care. For instance, the management of pregnant adolescents emerged as an area requiring further investigation to better understand current practices, challenges, and effective service delivery models for this sub-population. Peer support structures have been suggested as a potentially effective approach to improve adherence and retention among HIV-infected adolescents in resource-limited settings. However, further research is needed to validate this approach. Overall, this assessment highlights the wide variety of approaches currently being used to deliver adolescent HIV services in the region. Research is needed to identify which service delivery models are most effective in different contexts to improve retention, adherence, and treatment outcomes. Strengthening data recording systems across sub-Saharan Africa is critical to better monitor HIV-infected adolescents. Without this, it will remain challenging to conduct research and assess evidence-based approaches to improve the quality, uptake, and impact of adolescent HIV services. Acknowledgments are extended to individuals and organizations who contributed to this work, including experts from WHO, CHAI, USAID, CDC, EGPAF, EDC, the International HIV/AIDS Alliance, GNP+/Y+, PIH, the University of Oxford, the University of Kenya, Makerere University, and others. Special thanks are also given to the health facility staff who provided their time and valuable insights for this project. The research underscores the urgent need to develop and deliver antiretroviral treatment formulations tailored for infants and children with HIV/AIDS. It also highlights the importance of addressing the unique challenges faced by adolescents with perinatally acquired HIV, including mental health issues, adherence difficulties, and the transition to adult care services. The findings emphasize the necessity of integrating sexual and reproductive health services into HIV care and addressing the specific needs of pregnant adolescents. The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Paediatric AIDS Treatment for Africa (PATA) are collecting data to prepare for an Adolescent Technical Treatment meeting. This meeting aims to prioritize adolescent-specific content for the 2015 Consolidated ARV Guidelines update and support the development of a research agenda and strategy for adolescent HIV treatment. The research seeks to address the lack of information on the challenges clinics face in managing adolescent HIV care, particularly as this population faces unique issues related to long-term treatment and the transition to independence during adolescence. Clinics are encouraged to provide data to help WHO and PATA advocate for improved HIV treatment infrastructure and policies. The survey is voluntary, confidential, and designed to take approximately 10 minutes to complete. The findings will be shared with the PATA network to enhance understanding and support for adolescent HIV care.
